citations.quote: Fix a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put $$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$ Then: (a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and $\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and $c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate** $t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position** $r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair $(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$.

An **electric field of class $C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a **magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of the same class.

A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive.

The electric constant is defined within the framework by $$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$ in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$, so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$. (b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$ and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where $1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$ carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$. (c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram (kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$. (d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity with a similarly named quantity of another framework.

This is the same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is).

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$. This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Finite componentwise sums and products of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$, and a composite of composable $C^k$ Euclidean maps is $C^k$. Scalar multiples are included among the finite componentwise operations.

derivations.claim: The pair map $\Phi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^6$, $\Phi(x,t):=(E(x,t),B(x,t))$, is of class $C^k$ on the open set $\Omega\times I$ of [F1]: its six components are the components of the $C^k$ maps $E$ and $B$ of [F2]

The map $P:\mathbb R^6\to\mathbb R^4$, $P(e,b):=\bigl(\tfrac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\langle e,e\rangle+\tfrac{1}{2\mu_0}\langle b,b\rangle,\ \mu_0^{-1}\,e\times b\bigr)$, is of class $C^k$: each of its four components is a finite sum of scalar multiples of products of the coordinate functions $e_1,e_2,e_3,b_1,b_2,b_3$ and the constants $\varepsilon_0,\mu_0$, so repeated application of the algebra clause of [F5] exhibits it as $C^k$; the cross-product coordinate formula of [F4] identifies its last three components

Clause (a), units: with [F3] and [F4] the first summand of $u$ carries $(\mathrm C^2\,\mathrm N^{-1}\mathrm m^{-2})(\mathrm N\,\mathrm C^{-1})^2=\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$, because $|E|^2$ carries $(\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1})^2=(\mathrm N\,\mathrm C^{-1})^2$ and $\varepsilon_0$ carries $\mathrm F\,\mathrm m^{-1}=\mathrm C^2\,\mathrm J^{-1}\mathrm m^{-1}=\mathrm C^2\,\mathrm N^{-1}\mathrm m^{-2}$; the second summand carries $(\mathrm N\,\mathrm A^{-2})^{-1}(\mathrm N\,\mathrm A^{-1}\mathrm m^{-1})^2=\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$; and $S$ carries $(\mathrm N\,\mathrm A^{-2})^{-1}(\mathrm N\,\mathrm C^{-1})(\mathrm N\,\mathrm A^{-1}\mathrm m^{-1})=\mathrm N\,\mathrm A\,\mathrm C^{-1}\mathrm m^{-1}=\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-1}=\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm kg\,\mathrm s^{-3}$, using $\mathrm A=\mathrm C\,\mathrm s^{-1}$: the units asserted in clause (a) are exactly those of the two expressions

On $\Omega\times I$ the composite $P\circ\Phi$ equals $(x,t)\mapsto(u(x,t),S(x,t))$ of the Definition: its first component is $\tfrac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\langle E,E\rangle+\tfrac{1}{2\mu_0}\langle B,B\rangle=u(x,t)$, and its last three components are $\mu_0^{-1}E\times B=S(x,t)$. Since $\Phi$ and $P$ are of class $C^k$ by steps 1.1 and 1.2, the composition clause of [F5] makes the composite $C^k$, and the identification of components makes $u$ and $S$ of class $C^k$; this is clause (b)

Clause (c): for real $\lambda$, the bilinearity of [F4] gives $\langle\lambda E,\lambda E\rangle=\lambda^2\langle E,E\rangle$ and $(\lambda E)\times(\lambda B)=\lambda^2(E\times B)$, so $u$ and $S$ are homogeneous of degree two in the pair $(E,B)$, and $\varepsilon_0>0$, $\mu_0>0$ together with $|E|^2,|B|^2\ge0$ by [F3] and [F4] give $u\ge0$. No derivative of the fields and no further convention has entered clauses (a)-(c); clauses (d) and (e) record exclusions and status only, so the definition introduces no field equation and no physical interpretation

boundaries.reason: The definition is evaluated at points of the nonempty open region $\Omega\times I$; no empty family, empty indexing set or empty domain occurs in the claim.

boundaries.evidence: Step 3.1 substitutes $\lambda=0$ in the homogeneity identities $u(\lambda E,\lambda B)=\lambda^2u(E,B)$ and $S(\lambda E,\lambda B)=\lambda^2S(E,B)$, giving $u(0,0)=0=S(0,0)$; the zero field is therefore covered by the displayed formulas.

The definitions use one field pair $(E,B)$ and no family of fields; the case of a single summand is the only case and is treated by steps 1.1-2.1, where the polynomial expression has finitely many terms.
Step 3.1 covers vanishing components: if $E=0$ or $B=0$, the corresponding quadratic term drops and $S=0$ when either factor vanishes, with no nondegeneracy hypothesis on the fields.

boundaries.reason: The definition is pointwise on the open set $\Omega\times I$ and asserts nothing at boundary points of $I$ or $\Omega$; no interval endpoints arise.
The verification of clauses (a)-(c) is finite algebra over the field components (steps 1.1-3.1) and spends no choice principle; the mention of the weak branch in clause (g) records an exclusion only.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] A **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$ when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; then $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) $E$ is a **polar vector** and $B$ an **axial vector** relative to the
orientation of the spatial basis; the changes of inertial description adopted
for this framework are proper and orientation preserving, so
orientation-reversing descriptions are not among them.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], so
that $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$
is nonempty open, $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ is the position in the spatial chart,
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the frame basis of the spatial slice, and the spatial inner
product is the Euclidean form $\delta$; let the units and the constants $c>0$,
$\mu_0>0$ and $\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ be those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]]; let $k\ge1$, and let
$E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be an electric and a magnetic field of class
$C^k$ of [[def-em-fields]]. Write $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $|\cdot|$ for
the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
$\times$ for the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

(a) [Energy density and flux] The **electromagnetic energy density**
$u:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and the **energy flux density** (the **Poynting
vector**) $S:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are defined by

$$u(x,t):=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\,\langle E(x,t),E(x,t)\rangle+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\,\langle B(x,t),B(x,t)\rangle,\qquad S(x,t):=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\,E(x,t)\times B(x,t).$$

At fixed $t\in I$ the map $u(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is a real-valued
function on $\Omega$ and $S(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is a spatial vector
field on $\Omega$, read in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. The energy density
carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and
the energy flux density carries $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm s^{-3}$.

(b) [Regularity] If $E,B$ are of class $C^k$, then $u$ and $S$ are of class
$C^k$: they are the components of a polynomial expression in the components of
$E,B$, and the verification below exhibits the composite map. In particular $u$
and $S$ are continuous, and the definitions use no derivative of the fields.

(c) [Pointwise reading, quadratic character] The definitions use only the values
of $E$ and $B$ at the same point $(x,t)$, and they are quadratic in the fields:
for every real $\lambda$ one has $u(\lambda E,\lambda B)=\lambda^2u(E,B)$ and
$S(\lambda E,\lambda B)=\lambda^2S(E,B)$, and $u\ge0$. Consequently
decompositions of the fields do not make $u$ or $S$ additive; cross terms
generally contribute. No convention beyond the fixed laboratory frame enters
the definitions.

(d) [Products and singular support] If $E,B$ are only locally integrable (the
weak branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]), the products $E_iE_j$, $B_iB_j$ and
the components of $E\times B$ need not be locally integrable, and no product of
distributions is defined. The displayed formulas then define $u$ and $S$
pointwise almost everywhere, and the framework uses them only where the local
integrability of the products, respectively of the component being integrated,
is separately established. No value of $u$ or $S$ is assigned at a point of
singular source support.

(e) [Status] This item defines quantities only. The interpretation of $u$ as an
energy density and of $S$ as an energy flux density, and every balance identity
involving them, is the content of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] and of the other
balance items of this page; no identification of $(u,S)$ with components of a
covariant tensor is made here, and the relation $S=c^2g$ to the momentum density
$g$ of [[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]] is a consequence of those definitions,
not an identification made at this point.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $k\in\mathbb N$. Finite componentwise sums and products of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$, and a composite of composable $C^k$ Euclidean maps is $C^k$. Scalar multiples are included among the finite componentwise operations. The assertions remain valid on an empty open domain.

derivations.claim: Well-definedness and regularity. Each component $\sigma_{ij}$ of the displayed expression is a finite sum of scalar multiples of products of the component functions $E_iE_j$, $\lvert E\rvert^2=\sum_lE_lE_l$ and their $B$-analogues, together with the constant factor $\delta_{ij}$; these are $C^k$ functions of $(x,t)$ by [F2], [F5] and the product and sum clauses of [F7], so $\sigma:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is a $C^k$ tensor field. table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient

   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last

**Everything is proved through

(a) [Momentum density] The **electromagnetic momentum density** is the map
$g:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ defined by

$$g:=\frac{S}{c^2}=\varepsilon_0\,E\times B,$$

in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-2}\mathrm s^{-1}$; the second equality uses

(b) [Maxwell stress tensor] The **Maxwell stress tensor** is the spatial

$$\sigma_{ij}:=\varepsilon_0\Bigl(E_iE_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert E\rvert^2\Bigr)+\frac{1}{\mu_0}\Bigl(B_iB_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert B\rvert^2\Bigr),$$

derivatives being taken at fixed $t$.

(c) [Momentum flux] The **momentum flux tensor** is $\Pi:=-\sigma$, with
$(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\Pi_{ij}$; then
$\operatorname{div}\Pi=-\operatorname{div}\sigma$ componentwise.

(d) [Orbital angular momentum density and its flux] Relative to the origin of
the spatial chart, the **orbital angular momentum density** is
$\ell:=x\times g$, with components $\ell_i=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\epsilon_{ijk}x_jg_k$,
and its **flux tensor** is the spatial tensor field $x\times\Pi$ with
components

$$(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\epsilon_{ijk}\,x_j\,\Pi_{k\ell}.$$

Here $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the Levi-Civita symbol, defined by
$\epsilon_{ijk}=+1$ if $(i,j,k)$ is an even permutation of $(1,2,3)$,
$\epsilon_{ijk}=-1$ if it is an odd permutation, and $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$ if two
indices coincide, in the positively oriented basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. The object
$\ell$ carries $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-1}$ and the components
of $x\times\Pi$ carry $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm s^{-2}=\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-1}$.

(e) [Origin] Both $\ell$ and $x\times\Pi$ depend on the origin of the spatial
chart: under a shift $x\mapsto x+a$ of the origin by a constant $a\in\mathbb R^3$
their values become $\ell+a\times g$ and $x\times\Pi+a\times\Pi$ respectively,
so the definition fixes one origin in the laboratory frame and every statement
about $\ell$ or $x\times\Pi$ is relative to that fixed origin.

(f) [Status] This item fixes objects and index conventions only. No balance
identity and no interpretation of $\sigma$ or $\Pi$ as force or momentum flux
is asserted here; every balance identity involving these objects is the content
of the separate theorem items of this page.

(g) [Quadratic character and singular support] All four objects are quadratic
in the fields $E,B$. For a locally integrable branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] the exclusions recorded in
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]] apply to each of them: the products
$E_iE_j$, $B_iB_j$ and the components of $E\times B$ need not be locally
integrable, no product of distributions is defined, and the displayed formulas
then define the objects pointwise almost everywhere, the framework using them
only where the local integrability of the products is separately established.
No value is assigned at a point of singular source support.

(h) [No covariant object] No four-dimensional or covariant interpretation of
$(u,S,g,\sigma)$ is defined here; in particular $g$ is not identified with the
spatial components of a covariant momentum density.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), with coordinates $x_1,x_2,x_3$, partial derivatives $\partial_j=\partial/\partial x_j$, Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and norm $\lvert\cdot\rvert_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), divergence and curl as in [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and cross product as in [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. Put

$$Q_{ij}:=F_iF_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert F\rvert_2^2,\qquad \delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases}\qquad (\operatorname{div}Q)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_jQ_{ij}.$$

Then $Q$ is a $C^1$ tensor field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}Q=F\,\operatorname{div}F-F\times\operatorname{curl}F .$$

Moreover, writing $\epsilon_{ijk}$ for the Levi-Civita symbol ($\epsilon_{ijk}=+1$ if $(i,j,k)$ is an even permutation of $(1,2,3)$, $-1$ if it is an odd permutation, and $0$ if two indices coincide), every symmetric tensor $Q$ (that is, $Q_{kj}=Q_{jk}$ for all $j,k$) satisfies

$$\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}=0\qquad(i\in\{1,2,3\}),$$

the sum over $j,k$ being the nine-term sum with each pair counted separately. Finally, if $\Pi$ is a $C^1$ symmetric tensor field on $U$, if $g:U\to\mathbb R^3$ is continuous, and if $\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-f$ holds at every point of $U$ for a continuous $f:U\to\mathbb R^3$, where $(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_i=\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\partial_\ell\Pi_{i\ell}$ and $(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}:=\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\Pi_{k\ell}$ with the sum over $j,k$, then the vector field $x\times g$ and the tensor field $x\times\Pi$ satisfy

$$\partial_t(x\times g)+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi)=-x\times f .$$

No symmetry of $Q$ beyond the displayed form is assumed, and no boundary integral is asserted: these are pointwise identities on $U$.

**Set form.** Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, Lebesgue measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, let $a<b$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function, defined and continuous together with its partial derivative $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x),$$

and at $t=a$ and $t=b$ it has relative (one-sided) derivatives, taken within $[a,b]$, both equal to the same displayed integral. Equivalently, for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$,

$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{h_k}\Bigl(\int_Kf(x,t+h_k)\,d\lambda_n(x)-\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\Bigr)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$

**Surface form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. Let $S$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, and let $f$ be real-valued, defined and continuous together with $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$ is differentiable in the same relative sense with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)=\int_S\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma).$$

The statements are pointwise in $t$ and make no claim about moving parameter sets $K(t)$ or $S(t)$, about singularities crossing $K$ or $S$, about differentiability of $\partial_tf$, or about differentiation in the spatial variables; only the one-dimensional parameter $t$ is differentiated. Integrals are Lebesgue integrals, and the surface integrals are those of the cited surface measure; the case $K=\varnothing$ or $\lambda_n(K)=0$ is included and the two sides vanish.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If Omega has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$, with faces counted once off E. All integrals are finite. In a specified finite gluing, the two fluxes on every shared face cancel.
Let $m\ge1$, let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be a closed nondegenerate rectangle, and let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Its graph has content zero in $\mathbb R^{m+1}$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**
$q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the
sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is
not asserted.

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

(c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and
$j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the
charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model,
and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. (a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let $\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative $\partial_t$ at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], $$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$ (b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on $I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

The particle's own field is excluded from $F$: this is the external-field coupling, and it defines no self-force. (ii) [Continuum matter coupling] For a smooth source $(\rho,J)$ of [[def-em-sources]] interacting with the field through an explicitly stated matter model to which this coupling applies, adopt the force density $\rho E+J\times B$ (unit N m$^{-3}$) and the power density $J\cdot E$ (unit W m$^{-3}$) as the electromagnetic source terms of that matter model, with the spatial cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; they describe the local interaction of the field with matter and are not a property of a prescribed current alone. (iii) [Scope] The rest mass and the charge are inputs; $m$ is not derived within electromagnetism.

derivations.claim: Divergence of the stress tensor: define $Q^{(E)}_{ij}=E_iE_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert E\rvert^2$ and $Q^{(B)}_{ij}=B_iB_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert B\rvert^2$ at fixed time. Both are $C^1$ on the open $\Omega$, and [F4] applied to $F=E$ and to $F=B$ gives $\operatorname{div}Q^{(E)}=E\operatorname{div}E-E\times\operatorname{curl}E$ and $\operatorname{div}Q^{(B)}=B\operatorname{div}B-B\times\operatorname{curl}B$; since $\sigma=\varepsilon_0Q^{(E)}+\mu_0^{-1}Q^{(B)}$ and $\operatorname{div}$ is linear in its argument, $\operatorname{div}\sigma=\varepsilon_0(E\operatorname{div}E-E\times\operatorname{curl}E)+\mu_0^{-1}(B\operatorname{div}B-B\times\operatorname{curl}B)$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$.

Time derivative of the momentum density: because $g=\varepsilon_0E\times B$ and the components of $E\times B$ are finite sums of products of the component functions, the product rule and linearity [F2] give $\partial_t(E\times B)=\partial_tE\times B+E\times\partial_tB$ componentwise, hence $\partial_tg=\varepsilon_0(\partial_tE\times B+E\times\partial_tB)$ pointwise.

Fixed-volume setup: let $\Omega'$, $t_0<t_1$ be as in clause (b), fix $t\in(t_0,t_1)$ and choose $a,b$ with $t_0<a<t<b<t_1$. The closure $\overline{\Omega'}$ is compact and contained in the open $\Omega$, and each $g_i$ together with $\partial_tg_i$ is continuous on a neighbourhood of $\overline{\Omega'}\times[a,b]$ by [F3]; the boundary is Lebesgue-null by the finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and [F5], so integrals over $\Omega'$ and over its closure agree, and [F5] makes $t\mapsto\int_{\Omega'}g_i(x,t)\,dx$ differentiable at $t$ with derivative $\int_{\Omega'}\partial_tg_i(x,t)\,dx$.

Local identity: substitute [F1] into step 1.1: $\operatorname{div}\sigma=\rho E-\varepsilon_0E\times(-\partial_tB)-\mu_0^{-1}B\times(\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE)=\rho E+\varepsilon_0E\times\partial_tB-B\times J-(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}B\times\partial_tE$. By bilinearity and alternation of the cross product, $-B\times J=J\times B$ and $-(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}B\times\partial_tE=\varepsilon_0\,\partial_tE\times B$; hence $\operatorname{div}\sigma=\rho E+J\times B+\varepsilon_0(E\times\partial_tB+\partial_tE\times B)=f+\partial_tg$ by [F6] and step 1.2. Therefore $\partial_tg-\operatorname{div}\sigma=-f$, equivalently $\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-f$ because $\Pi=-\sigma$; this is clause (a).

Fixed-volume identity: by steps 1.3 and 2.1, for each $i$ we have $\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}g_i\,dx=\int_{\Omega'}\partial_tg_i\,dx=\int_{\Omega'}(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i\,dx-\int_{\Omega'}f_i\,dx$; the fixed-time vector field $x\mapsto(\sigma_{i1},\sigma_{i2},\sigma_{i3})(x,t)$ is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline{\Omega'}$ by [F3], so the divergence theorem of [F5] gives $\int_{\Omega'}(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i\,dx=\oint_{\partial\Omega'}\sum_j\sigma_{ij}n_j\,dS$ as a finite face sum. Substituting $\Pi=-\sigma$ turns this into the two displayed equalities of clause (b) under the stated $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

Clause (c) records the postulational status of the two inputs, the model dependence of $f$ and of the boundary term, and the exclusions inherited from the weak branch and from the coupling; the argument used only the adopted postulates, the definitions of $g,\sigma,\Pi$, the quadratic stress identity and the integration interface, and made no empirical claim.

Assume the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] and clause (ii) of
[[post-em-lorentz-coupling]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$
of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]: the fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are
jointly $C^1$ of [[def-em-fields]], the source fields $\rho,J$ are continuous
of [[def-em-sources]], the constants are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]],
the force density is
$f:=\rho E+J\times B$ of that clause (ii), in
$\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-3}$, and $g,\sigma,\Pi=-\sigma$ are the momentum
density, Maxwell stress and momentum flux of
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]. Then:

(a) [Local identity] On $\Omega\times I$, componentwise,

$$\partial_tg-\operatorname{div}\sigma=-f,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-f,$$

that is, $\partial_tg_i-\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\sigma_{ij}=-(\rho E_i+(J\times B)_i)$ for every $i$, with $\partial_t$ the partial derivative at fixed position and $\operatorname{div}$ taken at fixed time.

(b) [Fixed-volume identity] Let $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ be open with
$\overline{\Omega'}\subseteq\Omega$ carrying the finite piecewise $C^1$
presentation of
[[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], let
$t_0<t_1$ with $(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$

([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

**Set form.** Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, Lebesgue measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure $\lambda_n(K)<\infty$, let $a<b$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function, defined and continuous together with its partial derivative $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$ in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x),$$

and at $t=a$ and $t=b$ it has relative (one-sided) derivatives, taken within $[a,b]$, both equal to the same displayed integral. Equivalently, for every $t\in[a,b]$ and every sequence $h_k\to0$ with $h_k\ne0$ and $t+h_k\in[a,b]$,

$$\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{h_k}\Bigl(\int_Kf(x,t+h_k)\,d\lambda_n(x)-\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)\Bigr)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x).$$

**Surface form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the surface measure of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. Let $S$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, and let $f$ be real-valued, defined and continuous together with $\partial_tf$ on an open neighbourhood of $S\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)$ is differentiable in the same relative sense with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Sf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma)=\int_S\partial_tf(\sigma,t)\,dS(\sigma).$$

The statements are pointwise in $t$ and make no claim about moving parameter sets $K(t)$ or $S(t)$, about singularities crossing $K$ or $S$, about differentiability of $\partial_tf$, or about differentiation in the spatial variables; only the one-dimensional parameter $t$ is differentiated. Integrals are Lebesgue integrals, and the surface integrals are those of the cited surface measure; the case $K=\varnothing$ or $\lambda_n(K)=0$ is included and the two sides vanish.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If Omega has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$, with faces counted once off E. All integrals are finite. In a specified finite gluing, the two fluxes on every shared face cancel.
Let $m\ge1$, let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be a closed nondegenerate rectangle, and let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Its graph has content zero in $\mathbb R^{m+1}$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), with coordinates $x_1,x_2,x_3$, partial derivatives $\partial_j=\partial/\partial x_j$, Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and norm $\lvert\cdot\rvert_2$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), divergence and curl as in [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and cross product as in [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. Put

$$Q_{ij}:=F_iF_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert F\rvert_2^2,\qquad \delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases}\qquad (\operatorname{div}Q)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_jQ_{ij}.$$

Then $Q$ is a $C^1$ tensor field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}Q=F\,\operatorname{div}F-F\times\operatorname{curl}F .$$

Moreover, writing $\epsilon_{ijk}$ for the Levi-Civita symbol ($\epsilon_{ijk}=+1$ if $(i,j,k)$ is an even permutation of $(1,2,3)$, $-1$ if it is an odd permutation, and $0$ if two indices coincide), every symmetric tensor $Q$ (that is, $Q_{kj}=Q_{jk}$ for all $j,k$) satisfies

$$\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}=0\qquad(i\in\{1,2,3\}),$$

the sum over $j,k$ being the nine-term sum with each pair counted separately. Finally, if $\Pi$ is a $C^1$ symmetric tensor field on $U$, if $g:U\to\mathbb R^3$ is continuous, and if $\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-f$ holds at every point of $U$ for a continuous $f:U\to\mathbb R^3$, where $(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_i=\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\partial_\ell\Pi_{i\ell}$ and $(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}:=\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\Pi_{k\ell}$ with the sum over $j,k$, then the vector field $x\times g$ and the tensor field $x\times\Pi$ satisfy

$$\partial_t(x\times g)+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi)=-x\times f .$$

No symmetry of $Q$ beyond the displayed form is assumed, and no boundary integral is asserted: these are pointwise identities on $U$.

Retain the fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of [[def-em-fields]], the
energy density $u$ and Poynting vector $S$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]],
the laboratory region, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and its spatial
Euclidean structure of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the constants and units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and the partial derivatives $\partial_j$ of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Write $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ for the
position in the spatial chart, $\delta_{ij}$ for the Kronecker symbol
($\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise), $\lvert E\rvert^2=\langle E,E\rangle$
with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and
$\times$ for the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] in the frame
basis. Let $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $\mu_0>0$ be the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Momentum density] The **electromagnetic momentum density** is the map
$g:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ defined by

$$g:=\frac{S}{c^2}=\varepsilon_0\,E\times B,$$

in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-2}\mathrm s^{-1}$; the second equality uses
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

(b) [Maxwell stress tensor] The **Maxwell stress tensor** is the spatial
tensor field $\sigma$ on $\Omega\times I$ with components

$$\sigma_{ij}:=\varepsilon_0\Bigl(E_iE_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert E\rvert^2\Bigr)+\frac{1}{\mu_0}\Bigl(B_iB_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert B\rvert^2\Bigr),$$

in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$; the indices range over
$\{1,2,3\}$ and repeated symbols are not summed here, every sum being written
explicitly. The tensor is **symmetric**, $\sigma_{ij}=\sigma_{ji}$ for all
$i,j$, by inspection of the displayed expression. Its divergence is the vector
field with components
$(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$, the partial
derivatives being taken at fixed $t$.

(c) [Momentum flux] The **momentum flux tensor** is $\Pi:=-\sigma$, with
$(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\Pi_{ij}$; then
$\operatorname{div}\Pi=-\operatorname{div}\sigma$ componentwise.

(d) [Orbital angular momentum density and its flux] Relative to the origin of
the spatial chart, the **orbital angular momentum density** is
$\ell:=x\times g$, with components $\ell_i=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\epsilon_{ijk}x_jg_k$,
and its **flux tensor** is the spatial tensor field $x\times\Pi$ with
components

$$(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\epsilon_{ijk}\,x_j\,\Pi_{k\ell}.$$

Here $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the Levi-Civita symbol, defined by
$\epsilon_{ijk}=+1$ if $(i,j,k)$ is an even permutation of $(1,2,3)$,
$\epsilon_{ijk}=-1$ if it is an odd permutation, and $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$ if two
indices coincide, in the positively oriented basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. The object
$\ell$ carries $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-1}$ and the components
of $x\times\Pi$ carry $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm s^{-2}=\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-1}$.

(e) [Origin] Both $\ell$ and $x\times\Pi$ depend on the origin of the spatial
chart: under a shift $x\mapsto x+a$ of the origin by a constant $a\in\mathbb R^3$
their values become $\ell+a\times g$ and $x\times\Pi+a\times\Pi$ respectively,
so the definition fixes one origin in the laboratory frame and every statement
about $\ell$ or $x\times\Pi$ is relative to that fixed origin.

(f) [Status] This item fixes objects and index conventions only. No balance
identity and no interpretation of $\sigma$ or $\Pi$ as force or momentum flux
is asserted here; every balance identity involving these objects is the content
of the separate theorem items of this page.

(g) [Quadratic character and singular support] All four objects are quadratic
in the fields $E,B$. For a locally integrable branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] the exclusions recorded in
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]] apply to each of them: the products
$E_iE_j$, $B_iB_j$ and the components of $E\times B$ need not be locally
integrable, no product of distributions is defined, and the displayed formulas
then define the objects pointwise almost everywhere, the framework using them
only where the local integrability of the products is separately established.
No value is assigned at a point of singular source support.

(h) [No covariant object] No four-dimensional or covariant interpretation of
$(u,S,g,\sigma)$ is defined here; in particular $g$ is not identified with the
spatial components of a covariant momentum density.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The particle's own field is excluded from $F$: this is the external-field coupling, and it defines no self-force. (ii) [Continuum matter coupling] For a smooth source $(\rho,J)$ of [[def-em-sources]] interacting with the field through an explicitly stated matter model to which this coupling applies, adopt the force density $\rho E+J\times B$ (unit N m$^{-3}$) and the power density $J\cdot E$ (unit W m$^{-3}$) as the electromagnetic source terms of that matter model, with the spatial cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; they describe the local interaction of the field with matter and are not a property of a prescribed current alone. (iii) [Scope] The rest mass and the charge are inputs; $m$ is not derived within electromagnetism.
